items.originalTitle: Prevent cognitive debt by manually retyping LLM-generated code
items.summary:
A developer describes a workflow where they manually type out code generated by large language models (LLMs) instead of directly copying it, aiming to maintain a deep understanding of their projects and avoid accumulating cognitive debt. This approach slows down development compared to fully automated code generation but helps the developer build a mental model of the codebase, detect errors, and adapt the code to their preferences.

The developer instructs their coding assistant to show all proposed edits and commands in chat rather than modifying files directly, allowing them to review and enter changes manually. This method balances faster progress than coding without LLM assistance with greater comprehension than blindly accepting AI-generated code. The practice echoes traditional advice to type out code examples to learn effectively and is intended to preserve control and knowledge in an era of increasing AI involvement in software development.

items.title: AirLLM enables running 70B parameter large language models on a single 4GB GPU without quantization or pruning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AirLLM 70B inference with single 4GB GPU
items.summary:
AirLLM is a software tool that significantly reduces memory usage during inference, allowing large language models with up to 70 billion parameters to run on a single 4GB GPU. It achieves this without relying on quantization, distillation, or pruning techniques, and supports even larger models like Llama 3.1 405B on 8GB and DeepSeek-V3 671B on about 12GB by streaming sparse mixture-of-experts models one expert at a time.

The project includes features such as model compression for up to 3x inference speed improvements, support for various popular models including Llama 3.x/4, Qwen3, and others, and compatibility with MacOS. Recent updates have added support for extremely large models like Kimi K3 (2.8 trillion parameters) running on under 4GB of VRAM, leveraging expert streaming and requiring specific dependencies and CUDA versions. AirLLM is available as a Python package and integrates with Hugging Face model repositories for easy use.

items.title: Legal debate intensifies over whether AI-generated text qualifies as protected speech under the First Amendment and who must prove human authorship [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: If AI Outputs Aren't Speech, Who Has to Prove They're Human?
items.summary:
A recent wrongful-death lawsuit involving AI chatbot outputs has sparked legal debate about whether large language model (LLM) outputs constitute "speech" protected by the First Amendment. A federal judge allowed negligence claims to proceed, questioning if AI-generated text should receive constitutional protection, which could affect how such outputs are regulated.

Legal scholars argue over the doctrinal correctness of treating AI outputs as non-speech, focusing on whether human involvement in creating, selecting, or adopting the text determines First Amendment coverage. However, distinguishing human from machine-generated text at scale poses significant challenges, as current tools cannot reliably verify authorship, raising concerns about privacy, surveillance, and the burden on users and readers rather than developers.

The debate highlights the complexity of applying existing free speech laws to AI-generated content, with implications for regulation, user rights, and the future of digital expression. Courts and lawmakers face the challenge of balancing constitutional protections with the need to address harms linked to AI outputs, especially when human attribution is unclear or disputed.

items.originalTitle: Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI
items.summary:
On May 20, 2026, OpenAI announced that an internal AI model had found a counterexample to the longstanding "unit distance" problem posed by mathematician Paul Erdős in 1946. This marked the first significant proof generated by AI, introducing novel mathematical approaches and influencing subsequent problem-solving efforts. By August 1, OpenAI revealed that another unreleased model, Astra, had made ten additional mathematical advances, including solutions to three more Erdős problems, signaling a notable change in how AI contributes to mathematical research.

The progress was facilitated in part by English mathematician Thomas Bloom, who curated a comprehensive list of Erdős problems on erdosproblems.com, making them more accessible and better defined. Bloom's work helped bridge the gap between traditional mathematical challenges and modern AI techniques, enabling these models to tackle problems that had remained open for decades.

These developments have been recognized by mathematicians like Princeton's Noga Alon as a phase transition in AI's mathematical capabilities, potentially transforming research methodologies and accelerating the resolution of complex mathematical conjectures.

items.originalTitle: condense-json 1.0
items.summary:
Release: condense-json 1.0

I'm trying to get braver at releasing 1.0 versions. This little library is a year and a half old now - I've applied some sensible and non-disruptive fixes and shipped the big 1.0 for it.

Here's an example of what it can do, lifted from the README:

{ "foo": { "bar": { "string": "This is a string with foxes in it", "nested": { "more": ["Here is a string", "another with foxes in it too"] } } } }

Combine that with a replacements object:

{"1": "with foxes in it"}

And condense_json(input_json, replacements) produces the following:

{ "foo": { "bar": { "string": {"$r": ["This is a string ", {"$": "1"}]}, "nested": { "more": ["Here is a string", {"$r": ["another ", {"$": "1"}, " too"]}] } } } }

It scans for strings or substrings that are present in that replacements object and replaces those with a special {"$r": ...} syntax in the output.

You can reverse the effect with uncondense_json(condensed, replacements).

The idea is to make it easier to store JSON that includes duplicated data from other related structures. I use it to save space in the SQLite logs generated by LLM - see PR #1586 for the latest iteration of that.

items.originalTitle: Open letters about AI development
items.summary:
Open letters about AI development

I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well.

Open Weights and American AI Leadership was shepherded by Microsoft, dated July 24th, and signed by 235 AI-adjacent companies including NVIDIA (see Jensen's first ever tweet), Amazon, Y Combinator, The Linux Foundation, and (a later signer) OpenAI.

It's clearly an argument designed to counter any instincts by the current US government to ban or limit open weight models over "safety" concerns - a reasonable consideration given what happened to Claude Fable 5!

Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time.

The one surprising note in the letter is that it comes out in support of distillation, where models train on output from other models:

In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model-development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model’s outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation. It reflects a long tradition of learning from, building upon, and improving existing technologies, a tradition that has helped drive innovation since the rise of the open-source software movement.

Notably absent from the signatures: Anthropic, who published their own response Our position on open-weights models three days later. CEO Dario Amodei doubled down on the risk of authoritarian governments building "AI models that are more powerful than those built by the US", and models being "misused to carry out cyberattacks or biological attacks", and called for "a crack down on industrial-scale distillation operations", while also stating that "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models".

Then on July 28th Pacing the Frontier was published, featuring signatures from "1,324 employees of frontier AI companies" - with names like Jakub Pachocki (Chief Scientist, OpenAI), Ilya Sutskever (Safe Superintelligence Inc, previously OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Jack Clark (Anthropic) and more. Their core message:

We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.

Their concern is intense competitive pressure combined with accelerated AI progress caused by automated AI research - and given that Anthropic produce 80% of their code with Claude Code, OpenAI had Sol reduce their end-to-end serving costs by 20%, and Kimi K3 designed a chip to serve a nano model built on its own architecture, you can see why people are taking that risk more seriously right now.
